new_groups.label: London, 20 March 1771: Mr. Wilkes's letter to Sir Fletcher Norton: 'I this morning received an order commanding my attendance this day in the House of Commons ... In the name of the freeholders of Middlesex, I again demand my seat in Parliament'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter of John Wilkes to Sir Fletcher Norton, the Speaker of the House of Commons, dated London, 20 March 1771: 'I this morning received an order commanding my attendance this day in the House of Commons. I observe that no notice was taken of me in your order as a member of the House, and that I am not required to attend in my place ... In the name of the freeholders of Middlesex, I again demand my seat in Parliament ...'. Both Virginia Gazettes print it after a London paragraph of 22 March ('Mr. Wilkes, on Tuesday, having been served with an order to attend the House of Commons on Wednesday, wrote the following letter to Sir Fletcher Norton'); the Massachusetts Spy and the New-Hampshire Gazette print it under a heading of their own. A letter in its writer's words, as the papers reprinted it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1771 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1771 that reach 3 or more papers, and those of 1770 over the 1771 pages, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 71 items printed somewhere, 1 reaching 4 papers by the finder's counts; items_from_1770.json: 2). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1771 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (45 texts). For every text one paper short of the bar, the missing paper was looked for again on its pages, by the text's words (the best page within its weeks) and by its names (the pages holding three or more of its proper names), and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09): 15 clusters, each read. Every admitted item, and every item read one paper short of the bar outside the 45 texts, was then counted by phrase searches of its own words over all 546 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. Single paragraphs from runs of news are counted by their own words (C-09). In 1771 four papers survive only in January, from late April to May and in parts of June and July, when the Massachusetts Spy and Rind's Virginia Gazette both have issues: 1 item is printed by all four papers and admitted.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1771 has 4 catalogue series, which are 4 papers: the Massachusetts Spy (Boston; 25 issues, none from 2 February to 8 May or from 1 November to 18 December; a 26th filed under 1771 is the issue of 27 December 1770), the New-Hampshire Gazette and Historical Chronicle (Portsmouth; 50 issues, from 18 January), and two Virginia Gazettes, both printed at Williamsburg by different printers, Alexander Purdie and John Dixon (sn84024739; 48 issues) and William Rind (sn84024741; 12 issues, the last of 18 July). Papers in print in any three weeks: 4 in January, from late April to May and in parts of June and July; 3 or 2 in the rest of the year.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The admitted item was counted by phrase searches of its own words, every hit read; its papers are in the README's table of stories. The texts read and below the bar are listed in not_admitted with their counts.
counted_item_by_item.A page without a RevX transcription: The Massachusetts Spy of 9 May prints Mr. Wilkes's letter to Sir Fletcher Norton on a page that has no RevX transcription; the comparison by the opening missed it, and the look for the missing paper found it in the page's CA text, so the letter is in 4 of 4 and admitted; its excerpt there comes from the CA text.
counted_item_by_item.A letter and a paragraph on it: Three papers print an extract of a private letter from Constantinople ('The north east parts of Europe are at present both delighted and terrified ...'); the Massachusetts Spy prints, earlier and under another London date, a two-sentence paragraph of its own on what the letter says ('A LETTER from Constantinople says, That the Grand Seignor has at last taken the field in person ...'). As built, the paragraph recites part of the letter and is not counted as a printing of it (C-07), so the letter is in 3 of 4; counted as another printed form (C-02) it would be in 4 of 4 and admitted (for_user_decision).
counted_item_by_item.A notice quoted in other papers' words: The Commissary's notice to the clergy of Virginia of a convention on an American episcopate is printed whole by the two Virginia Gazettes; the Massachusetts Spy and the New-Hampshire Gazette print a paragraph of their own that quotes its passage on the episcopate, which is not a printing of the notice (C-06, C-07), so the notice is in 2 of 4.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs in runs of news: London news of the printers' case and the City's quarrel with the House of Commons (March to May 1771) reached the papers in runs of paragraphs and documents, each counted by its own opening (C-09): Mr. Wilkes's letter to the Speaker is printed by all four papers; the Guildhall Rota Book, the counsel's opinion, the case put to counsel, the Lord Mayor's habeas corpus and Lord Chatham's speech and motion are each in 3 of 4.
counted_item_by_item.Shared phrases that are not one item: Of the 15 clusters the sweep found in 4 papers, 6 are passages of Mr. Wilkes's letter, 1 is the Constantinople letter with the Spy's paragraph, 1 is the episcopate notice, and 7 are set phrases shared by different texts: the opening of addresses to governors ('May it please your Excellency, WE his Majesty's'), governors' titles, 'one of his Majesty's Justices of the Peace', an advertisers' formula, 'one of His Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State', 'at the Secretary of State's Office, in Cleveland Row' and 'the Lord Mayor and Mr. Alderman Oliver to the'. Two of the paragraphs under those phrases, a London report of the King of Spain's order for restoring Port Egmont and one that the City would meet on Tower-hill when Parliament was prorogued, were counted by their own words: each is in 3 of 4.

for_user_decision.The letter from Constantinople and the S: As built: the Massachusetts Spy's two-sentence paragraph on what a letter from Constantinople says (under London, 3 November 1770) recites part of the letter and is not counted as a printing of it (C-07), so the extract of the letter is in 3 of the 4 papers of its weeks and below the bar. If the owner counts the paragraph as another printed form of the letter (C-02, as the Hamburg letter printed in other words in 1772), the letter is in 4 of 4 and is admitted by the rule's first part, after a scan check of its printings: 1771 would have 2 stories.
for_user_decision.The floor of four papers where three sur: As built: four papers survive only in January, from late April to May and in parts of June and July; in the rest of the year two or three survive, so nothing printed only then reaches the bar of 4, as in 1770, 1772, 1789 and 1790. 1771 has one story, printed in May.
